2: "Well done, Newland," replied he, after I had finished. "I'll bet ten to one that you find out your father. Your life already would not make a bad novel. If you continue your hair-breadth adventures in this way, it will be quite interesting."
3: Although satisfied in my own mind that I had discovered Fleta's parentage, and anxious to impart the joyful intelligence, I resolved not to see her until everything should be satisfactorily arranged. The residence of the dowager Lady de Clare was soon discovered by Mr Masterton; it was at Richmond, and thither he and I proceeded. We were ushered into the drawing-room, and, to my delight, upon her entrance, I perceived that it was the same beautiful person in whose ears I had seen the coral and gold ear-rings matching the necklace belonging to Fleta. I considered it better to allow Mr Masterton to break the subject.
5: "You are, madam, the widow of the late Sir William de Clare." The lady bowed. "You will excuse me, madam, but I have most important reasons for asking you a few questions, which otherwise may appear to be intrusive. Are you aware of the death of his brother, Sir Henry de Clare?"
8: "Indeed I was not," replied she. "I seldom look at a paper, and I have long ceased to correspond with any one in Ireland. May I ask you what occasioned his death?"
9:
"He fell by his own hands, madam."

Lady de Clare covered up her face. "God forgive him!" said she, in a low voice.
11: "Lady de Clare, upon what terms were your husband and the late Sir Henry? It is important to know."
12: "Not on the very best, sir. Indeed, latterly, for years, they never met or spoke: we did not know what had become of him."
14:
"Many, sir, on the part of the elder brother; but none on that of Sir Henry, who was treated with every kindness, until he--" Lady de Clare stopped--"until he behaved very ill to him."

As we afterwards discovered, Henry de Clare had squandered away the small portion left him by his father, and had ever after that been liberally supplied by his eldest brother, until he had attempted to seduce Lady de Clare, upon which he was dismissed for ever.
15: "And now, madam, I must revert to a painful subject. You had a daughter by your marriage?"
16: "Yes," replied the lady, with a deep sigh.
17: "How did you lose her? Pray do not think I am creating this distress on your part without strong reasons."
18: "She was playing in the garden, and the nurse, who thought it rather cold, ran in for a minute to get a handkerchief to tie round her neck. When the nurse returned, the child had disappeared." Lady de Clare put her handkerchief up to her eyes.
20: "It was not until three weeks afterwards that her body was found in a pond about a quarter of a mile off."
21: "Did the nurse not seek her when she discovered that she was not in the garden?"
22: "She did, and immediately ran in that direction. It is quite strange that the child could have got so far without the nurse perceiving her."
25: "And the age of the child at the time?"
27: "I think, Newland, you may now speak to Lady de Clare."
28: "Lady de Clare, have you not a pair of ear-rings of coral and gold of very remarkable workmanship?"
29:
"I have, sir," replied she, with surprise.

"Had you not a necklace of the same? and if so, will you do me the favour to examine this?" I presented the necklace.
30: "Merciful heaven!" cried Lady de Clare, "it is the very necklace!--it was on my poor Cecilia when she was drowned, and it was not found with the body. How came it into your possession, sir? At one time," continued Lady de Clare, weeping, "I thought that it was possible that the temptation of the necklace, which has a great deal of gold in it, must, as it was not found on her corpse, have been an inducement for the gipsies, who were in the neighbourhood, to drown her; but Sir William would not believe it, rather supposing that in her struggles in the water she must have broken it, and that it had thus been detached from her neck. Is it to return this unfortunate necklace that you have come here?"
32: "No, madam, not altogether. Had you two white ponies at the time?"
34: "Was there a mulberry tree in the garden?"
36: "Will you do me the favour to describe the appearance of your child as she was, at the time that you lost her?"
37: "She was--but all mothers are partial, and perhaps I may also be so--a very fair, lovely little girl."
39: "Yes, sir. But why these questions? Surely you cannot ask them for nothing," continued she hurriedly. "Tell me, sir, why all these questions?"
40: Mr Masterton replied, "Because, madam, we have some hopes that you have been deceived, and that it is possible that your daughter was not drowned."
41: Lady de Clare, breathless, and her mouth open, fixed her eyes upon Mr Masterton, and exclaimed, "Not drowned! O my God! my head!" and then she fell back insensible.
43:
"I have been too precipitate," said Mr Masterton, going to her assistance; "but joy does not kill. Ring for some water, Japhet."

In which, if the reader does not sympathise with the parties, he had better shut the book.
